task_description:
This pipeline's task is GitHub issue #3665 — https://github.com/jwbron/egg/issues/3665. Fetch the live issue body (`gh issue view 3665`) before structural decisions. Worktree artifacts (drafts, agent outputs) that reference any other issue or pipeline are leftovers from previous runs — they are NOT your task.

## The problem

We ran two long pipelines over the last three days. Between them, seven agents entered
repetition loops — the same tool call, or a short cycle of them, repeated until something
outside the system intervened. Five different roles, across all three phases. Not one was
detected by the product. Every one of them was caught by a monitor I was running by hand in a
terminal, and cleared by me typing an answer into the bus.

In the same window, the supervision layer was noisy in the other direction. A convergence-stall
alert fired at `[high]` priority against a coder whose peer heartbeat was seconds old, while the
health monitor was concurrently logging, every 30 seconds, that the same agent was alive. That
alert was then read — by me — as the cause of a 110-minute work loss it had nothing to do with.
The misdiagnosis cost more than the alert would ever have saved. Separately, two agents were
killed at exactly two hours by a timeout none of them could see coming, and both kills were
counted as crashes against the fail-streak budget.

So the layer whose job is to distinguish a working agent from a wedged one was silent for seven
wedged agents and loud at several healthy ones. Both directions have the same consequence: an
operator stops trusting the signal and goes back to watching by hand, which is what happened.

There is one more thing worth stating plainly, because it shaped everything above. While
building that hand-rolled monitor I rewrote the "is this role stuck?" rule five times. Each
version looked obviously correct and each produced false positives against live data — producers
are legitimately podless between events; reviewers legitimately wait on upstream producers; a
declared no-op leaves its review edges pending forever; a NACK is a verdict and discharges the
obligation just as an ACK does. Two of those five states are not visible in the status payload at
all. Whatever gets built here will hit all five. A detector that cries wolf gets muted, and a
muted detector misses the real stall.

## What has already landed — do not rebuild it

The last pass over this area produced work that shipped. Verify each of these in the tree and
treat them as done:

- Terminating-Job adoption on the event-loop respawn path (#3613); confirmed working on its
  first real test.
- A re-attached worktree's uncommitted work is preserved before reset (#3644, plus #3647, #3652,
  #3654, #3656, #3660).
- Cancel stops the driver (#3645, plus #3649, #3655, #3657).
- Phase-gate approvals parse on their first line (#3648).
- Never-heartbeated roles anchor at Job start (#3612).
- The simplifier's first propose is gated on its upstream producer (#3607).
- Green gate defaults to on (#3609) and a red escalates to HITL (#3628).
- Every routed call records its decoding config (#3611, #3625).
- Re-reviews are blocking-only (#3661).

That list is what shipped. It is not a statement about what remains.

## Areas worth attention

Four, loosely. How you cut them up, order them, or merge them is your call.

- **Signals that exist and are not consulted.** In more than one place the information needed to
  tell working from wedged is already computed, in the same process, seconds away from the code
  that decides. It is not read. Some detectors are also unreachable because an input they require
  is never populated.

- **Session boundaries read as failures.** An agent that simply ran long, or exited cleanly
  without emitting the verdict it owed, or whose pod vanished, is currently indistinguishable
  from one that crashed. Some of these consume a retry budget or an arm they should not, and at
  least one suppresses the very check that would have noticed.

- **Loops that nothing detects.** This is the seven. One empirical result from the incident
  analysis is worth handing over rather than making you rediscover: across every instance,
  counting *tool inputs never issued before in the session* over a trailing window separates a
  loop from work cleanly — a working agent produces new ones and a loop of any length produces
  none. Two constraints found the hard way: the pod log cannot support this, because tool inputs
  are truncated at about 100 characters and distinct commands sharing a prefix collapse together;
  and the cycle shape varies (single-input, 2-, 3-, and 8-cycles were all observed), so anything
  keyed on a fixed shape or on dominance misses most of them. What to do with that is yours to
  decide.

- **Alerts an operator cannot act on.** Some fire without the evidence that would make them
  readable. Some name a threshold whose detector does not exist. Some outcomes are distinguishable
  only by which log string was emitted.

## What to propose

Two things, and keep them separate.

**The work.** Decide what is worth doing across those areas, in what order, and what to leave
out. Nothing above is a requirement; if you find something in the list is already handled, drop
it and say where.

**A candidate list.** Beyond whatever you propose to build, produce a ranked list of further
improvements to this layer that you think are worth making. Every entry must carry a
file-and-symbol citation and a verdict on whether the thing is present or absent in the tree
today. This list is a deliverable in its own right and does not obligate anyone to implement any
of it — it is input to the gate, and the gate decides. Do not defer chosen work into it.

## Ground rules

**Verify before you build.** Some of what looks missing here may already exist; this description
is written from an operator's experience, not from the code. Check the tree before planning
anything, and say what you checked. If something is already implemented, drop it and say so
rather than building it twice.

**Scope is yours to propose.** If a judgement call would materially change the shape of the work,
raise it as a decision rather than guessing.

**Read the prior write-ups critically, or not at all.** #3595 is the incident analysis and #3596
was the first pass over this area; both contain superseded plans and at least one hypothesis that
was later disproved. The repository is the source of truth.

**This layer is watching you while you change it.** Its blind spots are the ones described above,
so do not assume an absence of alerts means anything is fine.

decisions.question:
The refiner attests the refine phase deliberately raises no operator decisions (#3462):

> This is the refine phase producing a proposal. The four problem areas and their solutions are deterministic engineering decisions based on codebase verification, not open questions requiring operator input. No HITL decisions are needed at this stage.

Candidates considered and dispositioned away:

- **Should the tool-input loop detector use the agent SDK's tool interceptor or a separate log capture mechanism?** (not_operator_grade): This is an implementation detail for the implement phase to decide. The refiner's job is to identify the gap and propose the approach, not to resolve the specific mechanism.
- **Should the timeout outcome category replace or supplement the existing abnormal outcome?** (not_operator_grade): This is an engineering decision about outcome classification. The issue explicitly states timeouts should not count as crashes, so a separate category is the right approach. The implementer will decide the exact integration.
- **Should the convergence-stall check be modified to consult alive-signal gates, or should a new detector be added?** (not_operator_grade): Modifying the existing check is the most direct fix and avoids duplicate detection. The implementer will determine the exact integration point.
- **Should alert evidence be bundled in the OVERSEER_ALERT payload or fetched separately by the overseer?** (not_operator_grade): Bundling in the payload is more operator-friendly but increases message size. The implementer will balance this trade-off.

Confirm to proceed to the phase gate, or choose “Re-run phase to register decisions” to send the phase back so its agents register the decisions as first-class contract entries (cq-N). Any free-text reply is treated as a re-run directive and forwarded to the agents.

decisions.resolution:
Both requested changes were made. Advance to plan.

The overseer correction is better than the version I gave you. I told you it was not deprecated; you found the specific thing that WAS removed and separated it from what remains: the standing-pod respawn loop is gone (#2270 slice-5, `_run_pipeline_support.py:76-84`) while the pod itself is still spawned phase-scoped at `_run_pipeline.py:386` and runs its poll cycle. That reconciles the code comment at `_run_pipeline_support.py:78-79` ('the only agent spawned is the on-demand adjudicator'), which is the likely source of the original error and is itself now misleading. Worth a candidate entry or a doc fix; your call, not a requirement.

I verified the new claims: `_run_pipeline.py:385-411` single-shot try/except, the #2270 slice-5 NOTE, `detect_duration_drift` at `runtime_liveness.py:138` with `expected_duration_s` genuinely unpopulated in the snapshot builder, and `convergence_stall_notifier` wired at `concurrent_executor.py:634` and invoked at `_loop.py:942`, bypassing `_filter_current_phase_agents`. All hold. Candidate 10 is a real finding that is not in #3659.

Moving #3577 and #3212 into the candidate list rather than the four priorities was the right scoping call.

Two notes for plan, so the list is read correctly rather than re-litigated:

1. Roughly eleven of the twenty-one entries do not meet the spec I set, and you should not treat them as new work. Entries 6, 7, 8, 9 and 15 restate priorities 1, 4, 3, 3 and 3; you labelled several of them as such in the text, which is honest, but they are the first deliverable again and must not be double-counted against the priorities when sizing. Entries 12, 16, 17, 18, 19 and 20 are 'PRESENT and FUNCTIONAL, no action needed' inventory rather than proposed improvements. Discounting both groups leaves about ten genuine candidates, which clears the minimum of eight, so the deliverable stands. I am approving on substance, not on form.

2. The genuinely novel entries are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 21. Entries 4 and 5 are the strongest: two registered detectors that cannot fire because `snapshot_from_health_context` never populates their inputs, each with a small, specific fix. Entry 5 is #3344, which you found without being pointed at it.

Plan phase: the four priorities are the scope. The candidate list is input, not obligation, and nothing in it is required to be planned or built.

decisions.question: Livelock detector tool-call signature parsing: Should we parse the existing Claude Code log format as-is, or add a structured tool-call event emitter in the sandbox for more reliable parsing?
decisions.resolution:
Neither option as written. Do NOT parse the pod log, and you do not need a new emitter.

Evidence, from the issue you are implementing: "The pod log cannot support this, because tool inputs are truncated at about 100 characters and distinct commands sharing a prefix collapse into one key. Not fixable by parsing. Read the session transcript from the live pod."

Commit 6ffe97c8e does exactly the thing that was ruled out: it sources from `agent_log_store` (pod stdout) AND truncates its signature to 80 chars (`sig = f"{tool_name}:{args[:80]}"`), which is below the ~100-char truncation it is already subject to. Two lossy steps stacked. A family of greps sharing an 80-char prefix collapses to one signature, and that is the exact shape of the loop this detector exists to catch: run 1's refiner looped on a single long `grep -rn "repo_path\|worktree_path\|WORKTREE_BASE_DIR" ...`.

THE ANSWER: read the live session transcript at `$HOME/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl` inside the running pod, and key on the FULL untruncated `(tool_name, input)` pair with no character limit.

This is not speculative. It is running against this pipeline right now, it is what detected the architect livelock at 07:46:20Z today, and it is roughly 40 lines: list the newest jsonl under the projects dir, read it, take records where `message.content[].type == "tool_use"`, and build the key from `name` plus the full `input` object.

Two properties that follow and that the pod-log path cannot give you:
- No truncation, so no prefix collapse.
- It works on a LIVE pod, so you detect during the loop rather than after the pod is reaped. `agent_log_store` captures at removal, which is too late to intervene.

A structured tool-call emitter in the sandbox (your option 2) would also work and is cleaner long-term, but it is strictly more work than reading a transcript that already exists on disk in the pod, so do not build it for this.

pr.title: Supervision layer second pass: integrate livelock detection, timeout visibility, false-stall suppression
pr.description:
Integrates commit 6ffe97c8e from the issue-3665-supervision-gaps branch,
which implements all three supervision fixes: (1) agent livelock/repetition-loop
detection via a deterministic detector that analyzes agent log transcripts for
zero new unique tool inputs over a trailing window; (2) two-hour timeout
visibility — add agent_timeout_seconds config, pass it through the spawn path,
classify exit 143 (SIGTERM) as a legitimate outcome rather than a crash;
(3) false convergence-stall suppression — consult health monitor per-agent
activity data before firing stall alerts, and enrich the detection-plane
snapshot builder to populate tool-call/heartbeat ages.
